title: The fair value of a dice sum
objectives: Price a dice outcome by its expectation.

screens.title: One die
screens.prose: The interviewer rolls one fair die. They offer a contract that pays £1 for every pip showing. The bars show the chance of each face.
screens.question: What is the most you can pay for it without losing on average, in pounds?

hints.text: Imagine 600 rolls. About how many of each face come up?
Each face comes up about 100 times in 600 rolls.
The 600 rolls pay about $100 \times 21 = 2{,}100$ pounds, so £3.50 a roll.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each payout by its chance of 1/6 and add.

byKey.middle: There is no single middle face: 3 and 4 share the middle. The average sits halfway, at 3.5.
byKey.best: That is what the contract pays on its best roll. Most rolls pay less.
byKey.worst: That is the worst roll. Paying only that leaves money on the table.

explain.text: Each face has chance 1/6, so the average payout is $21/6 = 3.5$ pounds. No single roll pays £3.50. It is the average over many rolls, and paying more than that loses money on average.

screens.title: Two dice
screens.prose: Now the contract pays the total of two dice, in pounds. Roll the dice in batches and watch where the average total settles.
screens.question: Roll 1,000 pairs. Where does the average total settle?

options.why: You put the range at 1 to 12. Two dice total at least 2, so halfway is 7.
A finite run wanders around 7. Only the long-run average is exactly 7.

options.text: Near the top, because 12 pays most.
options.why: You weighted the big payout by its size alone. A 12 comes up only 1 time in 36.

hints.text: Totals near the middle come up most often.
The bars are symmetric about 7.
Each die averages 3.5, so the total averages $3.5 + 3.5 = 7$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look where the bars balance.

explain.text: The bars are symmetric about 7, so they balance there. Each die averages 3.5, and the averages add: 7. A batch of 1,000 lands close to 7, not exactly on it.

screens.title: Three dice
screens.prose: The long-run average payout is the contract’s **fair value**: its expectation $E[X]$. Pay less and you gain on average; pay more and you lose. Now the contract pays the total of three dice.
screens.question: What is the fair value, in pounds?

hints.text: What does each die add on average?
The fair value of each die is 3.5, and fair values add.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the fair value of each die.

byKey.mode: You picked a most likely total. 10 and 11 each have 27 ways in 216; the fair value sits between them.
byKey.mode11: You picked a most likely total. 10 and 11 each have 27 ways in 216; the fair value sits between them.
byKey.mid: You used 3 as each die’s middle. Each die averages 3.5, not 3.

explain.text: Each die adds 3.5 on average, so three dice give 10.5. The two tallest bars, 10 and 11, straddle it. A fair value need not be a total you can roll.

screens.title: Counting sixes
screens.prose: The interviewer rolls three dice. This contract pays £10 for each six that shows. The bars show how many sixes come up.
screens.question: What is its fair value, in pounds?

widget.accept: £5: each die pays £10 with chance 1/6, so £10/6 a die and £5 for three.
widget.label: Fair value in pounds

hints.text: Price one die first: what does it pay on average?
One die pays £10 with chance 1/6: $10/6$ pounds on average.
Three dice: $3 \times 10/6 = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each die alone, then add.

byKey.at-least-one: You priced at least one six: $10 \times 91/216$. Two or three sixes pay more, so count every six.
byKey.one-die: That is one die’s worth. There are three dice, and fair values add.
byKey.most-likely: No sixes is the most likely result, but the others pay. Weight every result by its chance.

explain.text: Each die pays £10 with chance 1/6, worth $10/6$ pounds. Three dice add to £5, however the sixes fall. From the bars, $(10 \times 75 + 20 \times 15 + 30 \times 1)/216 = 1{,}080/216 = 5$ as well.

screens.title: The larger of two
screens.prose: Two dice. This contract pays the larger of the two faces. The larger is $k$ in $2k - 1$ of the 36 rolls, so the bars climb.

state.caption: The larger face: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11 rolls in 36

screens.question: What is its fair value? Give four decimal places, or a fraction.

hints.text: Weight each value $k$ by $(2k-1)/36$.
The top value, 6, has 11 rolls of the 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each value by its number of rolls, add, and divide by 36.

byKey.one-die: That is one die. Taking the larger of two pushes the value up.
byKey.mode: You priced the most likely value, 6. Five other values pay less.
byKey.mid: Guessing halfway up is not a price. Weight each value by its rolls.

explain.text: Each value times its rolls gives 1, 6, 15, 28, 45 and 66, which add to 161. So the fair value is $161/36 \approx 4.4722$. The most likely value, 6, is well above it.

screens.title: One die, used twice
screens.prose: Contract A pays the product of two different dice. Its fair value is $3.5 \times 3.5 = 12.25$. Contract B rolls **one** die and pays its face times itself.

state.caption: Contract A uses all 36 cells. Contract B uses only the diagonal.

screens.question: What is the fair value of contract B? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: Contract B can only land on the shaded diagonal.
Six equally likely payouts: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List contract B’s six payouts and average them.

byKey.product-of-means: You multiplied the fair values, 3.5 × 3.5. That works only for independent dice, and one die is not independent of itself.
byKey.square-sum: That is the total of the six payouts. Divide by 6 for the average.

explain.text: Contract B pays 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 or 36, each with chance 1/6: $91/6 \approx 15.17$. Multiplying fair values works only for independent dice. The gap, $91/6 - 49/4 = 35/12$, is exactly one die’s variance.

screens.title: How far it strays
screens.prose: The interviewer also asks how far a total strays from its fair value. One die has variance $35/12$. For independent dice, the variances add.
screens.question: Fill in the variance and the standard deviation (sd). Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Add one die’s variance for each die.
Two dice: $2 \times 35/12 = 35/6 \approx 5.8333$.
Take each square root last: $\sqrt{35/6} \approx 2.4152$ and $\sqrt{35/4} \approx 2.9580$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the variances, then take the square root.

byKey.r1c2: Take the root of the variance: $\sqrt{5.8333} \approx 2.4152$. If you wrote 3.4157, you added the sds.
byKey.r2c2: Take the root of the variance: $\sqrt{8.75} \approx 2.9580$. If you wrote 5.1235, you added the sds.

explain.text: Variances add: $35/6$ for two dice and $35/4$ for three. The sds are their roots, 2.4152 and 2.9580. Adding sds would give 3.4157 and 5.1235, far too wide.

screens.title: Why variances add
screens.prose: Why did you add variances and not sds? Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be two independent dice.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order, and leave out the false step.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}(X_1 + X_2) = \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(X_2) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(X_1, X_2)$, by expanding the square

lines.why: Spreads do not add. Variances add for independent dice, so the sd is the root of the sum.

hints.text: Start from the general rule for the variance of a sum.
Independence removes the covariance term.
Expand, drop the covariance, put in 35/12, then take the root.

feedback.correct: Expand, drop the covariance, substitute, then root.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the variance of a sum and take the root only at the end.

byKey.bad: Spreads do not add. Variances add for independent dice, so the sd is the root of the sum.
byKey.left-out: Every true line belongs in the derivation. Only the line about adding spreads is false.

explain.text: The covariance term vanishes for independent dice, so the variances add to $35/6$. The sd is its root, 2.4152. Roots do not add: $\sqrt{a + b}$ is less than $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$.

screens.title: Any number of dice
screens.prose: Every contract you priced used two rules. For the total $S_n$ of $n$ independent dice, $$E[S_n] = 3.5n, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(S_n) = \sqrt{\tfrac{35}{12}\,n}$$ The fair value grows like $n$, the spread only like $\sqrt{n}$.
screens.question: A contract pays the sum of 100 dice. Which fair value and sd are right?

options.why: You multiplied one die’s sd by 100. Variances add, so the sd grows like $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
That is the variance, $100 \times 35/12$. Take its square root.
You used 3 for each die. Each die averages 3.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the fair value by 100 and the variance by 100.

explain.text: The fair value is $3.5 \times 100 = 350$, and the sd is $\sqrt{100 \times 35/12} \approx 17.08$. With 100 dice the total is very close to normal. So 350 ± 17 holds about two thirds of outcomes.

hints.text: `product(range(1, 7), repeat=n_dice)` lists every roll as a tuple.
Add `outcome_fn(roll)` over all rolls and divide by how many there are, as a Fraction.
For the sd, the variance is $35n/12$: return `sqrt(Fraction(35, 12) * n)`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Average the payout over every roll with Fraction, and add variances for the sd.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
`fair_value` averages the payout over all $6^n$ equally likely rolls, so it is exact for any contract. `sd_of_sum` adds one die’s variance per die, then takes the root. Your function confirms 161/36 for the larger die and 91/6 for the square.

```python
rolls = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=n_dice))
return Fraction(sum(outcome_fn(r) for r in rolls), len(rolls))
```

screens.question: What is your P&L at the fair value, in pounds?

widget.accept: £2: each sale is £1 above fair value, and you sold 2.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

hints.text: How far above fair value did you sell?
Each unit sold at 11.50 against a value of 10.50: £1 each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A seller makes the price minus the value, on each unit.

byKey.sign: You sold above the value, so you gain. Price minus value is +£1 a unit.
byKey.one: That is one unit. The interviewer bought 2.
byKey.cash: That is the cash you received. Subtract what the 2 contracts are worth, £21.

explain.text: Each sale is £1 above fair value, so the ledger shows +£2. If the dice then come 14, you lose $2 \times 2.50 = 5$ pounds on the day. That loss is luck: at the price you sold, the trade was worth +£2.

screens.title: The charity game
screens.prose: A charity trading game lists a contract on the sum of three dice, rolled at the end. The last game’s total was 15. The first trader asks you where your price is centred.

state.caption: The dice have no memory of the last game

screens.question: Where do you centre your first quote?

options.text: At 10.5, the fair value of three dice.
At 10 or 11, the most likely totals.
options.why: You centred on the most likely total. A price centres on the fair value, which weighs every total.

options.text: At 13, because high totals are running.
options.why: You let the last game move your price. Fresh dice do not remember 15.
The lowest total is 3, not 0. Halfway between 3 and 18 is 10.5.

hints.text: What is the long-run average total of three dice?
Each die averages 3.5, whatever happened last game.
Centre at $3 \times 3.5 = 10.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre the price on the fair value.

explain.text: The fair value of three fresh dice is 10.5, whatever the last game showed. Your quote sits around it, perhaps 9.5 to sell to you and 11.5 to buy from you. Lesson 5 makes that two-sided price exact.

ideas: A contract’s fair value is its expected payout: what you would pay to break even on average.
Fair values add: one die 3.5, two dice 7, three dice 10.5. Variances add too, so the sd grows like $\sqrt{n}$.
Multiply fair values only for independent dice: one die squared is worth 91/6, not 12.25.
summary.trap: Pricing a contract at its most likely value, or multiplying fair values for a die used twice.
